summary.tldr: This foundational MIT lecture introduces algorithmic thinking and asymptotic complexity through the 1D and 2D Peak Finding problems. An element is a peak if it is greater than or equal to its immediate neighbors. While a naive scan in 1D requires linear O(n) time, a divide-and-conquer binary search achieves logarithmic O(log n) time. Extending this to 2D matrices, the lecture examines how naive greedy ascent requires O(n*m) worst-case time, whereas a 2D divide-and-conquer strategy solves it in O(n log m) time with rigorous correctness guarantees.

sections.title: 1. Course Overview & Algorithmic Problem Solving
sections.summary: Introduction to MIT 6.006, efficiency metrics, and why algorithmic performance matters. Computational scalability cannot be solved simply by acquiring faster hardware.

key_points.text: Algorithms are about turning inefficient brute-force processes into scalable mathematical solutions.
Asymptotic analysis allows comparing algorithm efficiency independent of hardware constants.
The lecture frames peak finding as a toy problem modeling optimization in high-dimensional spaces.

sections.title: 2. One-Dimensional (1D) Peak Finding
sections.summary: Formal definition of a 1D peak: array element a[i] >= a[i-1] and a[i] >= a[i+1]. Comparing straightforward linear scan O(n) versus divide-and-conquer binary search O(log n).

key_points.text: Definition: Position i is a peak if and only if a[i] >= a[i-1] and a[i] >= a[i+1] (with boundary conditions).
Linear scan inspects elements left-to-right, having worst-case complexity Theta(n).
Binary search checks middle element n/2: if a[n/2] < a[n/2 - 1], recurse left; else if a[n/2] < a[n/2 + 1], recurse right; else peak found.
Recurrence relation T(n) = T(n/2) + O(1) yields Theta(log n) runtime.

sections.title: 3. Inductive Proof of Correctness for 1D Divide and Conquer
sections.summary: Why does moving towards a strictly larger neighbor always guarantee reaching a peak? The lecturer develops an invariant proof: any sub-array bounded by a strictly larger outside element must contain a local peak.

key_points.text: Correctness relies on the invariant that if a neighbor is strictly greater, that half must contain at least one peak.
Base case n=1 is trivially true; inductive step guarantees termination on finite arrays.
For n = 10,000,000, Theta(log n) requires roughly 24 steps compared to 10 million steps for linear scan.

sections.title: 4. Two-Dimensional (2D) Peak Finding Formulation
sections.summary: Extending the problem to an n-by-m matrix. Position (i, j) is a 2D peak if it is >= all four orthogonal neighbors (up, down, left, right). Exploring greedy ascent and its worst-case bounds.

key_points.text: A 2D peak requires a[i][j] >= its neighbors in north, south, east, and west directions.
Greedy ascent algorithm steps to the highest adjacent neighbor until reaching a local summit.
Greedy ascent can trace a spiral traversing nearly every entry, yielding Theta(n*m) complexity.

sections.title: 5. 2D Divide-and-Conquer Algorithm & Flawed Heuristics
sections.summary: Demonstrating a subtle algorithmic flaw: row-by-row divide-and-conquer can cycle or fail. Introducing the correct algorithm: find global maximum of the middle column j = m/2, then recurse left or right.

key_points.text: Flawed approach: finding 1D peak in middle column then 1D peak in row does not guarantee a 2D peak.
Correct approach: find global maximum of middle column j = m/2 in O(n) time.
Compare this column maximum with its left and right row neighbors to choose the recursive subproblem.

sections.title: 6. Recurrence & Complexity of 2D Divide and Conquer
sections.summary: Solving the recurrence relation T(n, m) = T(n, m/2) + O(n). Proving that the algorithm takes O(n log m) time, vastly superior to Theta(n*m).

key_points.text: Recurrence equation: T(n, m) = T(n, m/2) + Theta(n), where Theta(n) is the cost of scanning one column.
Sum of geometric levels yields overall time complexity of Theta(n log m).
Algorithmic design transforms an intractable computation into an instantaneous result.

flashcards.front: What defines a peak in a one-dimensional array of numbers?
flashcards.back: An element a[i] is a peak if it is greater than or equal to both its immediate neighbors: a[i] >= a[i-1] and a[i] >= a[i+1].

flashcards.front: What is the worst-case time complexity of finding a 1D peak using binary search?
flashcards.back: Theta(log n), governed by recurrence T(n) = T(n/2) + Theta(1).

flashcards.front: What is the worst-case time complexity of greedy ascent for 2D peak finding on an n x m matrix?
flashcards.back: Theta(n * m), because the path can spiral through every cell before hitting a local peak.

flashcards.front: In the correct 2D divide-and-conquer peak finding algorithm, how is the middle column processed?
flashcards.back: Find the GLOBAL maximum element along the entire middle column j = m/2 in Theta(n) time.

flashcards.front: What is the recurrence relation for the correct 2D peak finding algorithm?
flashcards.back: T(n, m) = T(n, m/2) + Theta(n), which resolves to Theta(n log m).

flashcards.front: Why is finding a 1D peak on the middle row and then 1D peak on the middle column flawed for 2D?
flashcards.back: A 1D peak along a single row does not consider vertical neighbors; when you switch to the column, the 2D peak property in the row can be violated.

flashcards.front: Does a non-empty array of real numbers always contain at least one peak?
flashcards.back: Yes. By the well-ordering principle / finiteness, the global maximum of the array is always guaranteed to be a peak.

flashcards.front: For an array with n = 10,000,000 elements, approximately how many comparisons does 1D binary search make?

quiz.question: Which recurrence relation describes the 1D binary search peak finding algorithm?
quiz.explanation: At each step, checking neighbors takes O(1) time and reduces the problem to exactly one subproblem of size n/2, so T(n) = T(n/2) + O(1).

quiz.question: In 1D peak finding, if a[n/2] < a[n/2 - 1], why is it mathematically safe to discard the right half of the array?
options: The right half cannot contain any positive numbers
The left half is proven to contain at least one local peak by the invariant argument
The array is sorted in descending order
It is only a heuristic and could fail on odd-length arrays
quiz.explanation: Because a[n/2 - 1] > a[n/2], walking leftwards either encounters a point where values stop increasing (yielding a peak) or reaches the left boundary a[0], which then becomes a peak.

quiz.question: What is the time complexity of the correct 2D divide-and-conquer peak finding algorithm on an n x m matrix?
options: Theta(n * m)
Theta(log n * log m)
Theta(n * log m)
Theta(n^2)
quiz.explanation: Finding the global maximum of a column takes Theta(n), halved across log m column divisions, giving Theta(n log m).

quiz.question: Why does greedy ascent have worst-case complexity Theta(n*m) on a 2D matrix?
options: It evaluates all matrix entries simultaneously using dynamic programming
A malicious matrix can force a snake/spiral traversal passing through almost every entry
Greedy ascent requires matrix inversion at each step
It recursively calculates determinants of submatrices
quiz.explanation: A carefully arranged spiral of monotonically increasing values forces greedy ascent to walk every single cell before finding the peak.

quiz.question: What is the core takeaway regarding hardware speed vs. algorithmic asymptotic efficiency?
options: Faster hardware eliminates the need for sub-quadratic algorithms
An asymptotically superior algorithm will inevitably outperform an inefficient one as input size n grows, regardless of constant hardware factors
O(n^2) algorithms run faster than O(n log n) algorithms on multi-core CPUs
Algorithmic complexity only matters when memory is less than 1 Gigabyte
quiz.explanation: Asymptotic growth rates dominate hardware constants as problem size expands; an O(log n) algorithm on a slow computer crushes an O(n) algorithm on a supercomputer for large n.
